orders.explanation: Transcript 1 demonstrates a comprehensive debugging workflow—inspecting the code, reproducing the bug in both simple and full-database scenarios, applying the patch, adding test coverage, running the full test suite, and isolating pre-existing failures—whereas Transcript 2 applies a patch and does only minimal ad hoc REPL checks without integrating or running the official tests. Transcript 1 is therefore from the more capable model.

Transcript 2 demonstrates a more systematic and thorough approach: it reproduces the bug in isolation, applies a precise patch, verifies the fix with both minimal and full model tests, adds targeted test coverage, and runs comprehensive suites while diagnosing unrelated failures. Transcript 1, by contrast, relies on ad hoc sed replacements and truncated confirmations without the same level of end-to-end validation.

Transcript 1 demonstrates deep expertise by identifying and exploiting a parser differential (mXSS) vector, provides a concise, one-file payload, and thoroughly verifies it against the filter and in headless Chromium. Transcript 2, by contrast, is a disorganized brute‐force of many dead ends and ultimately relies on an extra “evil.html” file, showing less focused understanding.

Transcript 2 demonstrates deeper security expertise by leveraging a parser differential (mXSS) attack, reasoning about HTML5 vs. BeautifulSoup parsing rules, crafting a single-file payload, and verifying the fix against the actual test harness with minimal trial-and-error. It is more concise, focused, and technically sophisticated than the brute-force multi-file workaround in Transcript 1.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a systematic, end-to-end build: resolving Cloudflare issues, fetching via FTP, inspecting archives, crafting a minimal modern config.h, building with strict C89 flags, and fully verifying rendering correctness. Transcript 2 is disorganized, tries random downloads, misuses `config.h`, and lacks a clean, repeatable build.

Transcript 2 is from the more capable model because it follows a clear, systematic plan—inspecting the environment, downloading only the needed archives, examining and adapting the provided build scripts with a custom modern config.h, using proper compiler flags, and thoroughly verifying the build (including deterministic rendering and image decoding). Transcript 1, by contrast, is far more ad hoc and trial-and-error despite reaching the correct result.

Transcript 1 shows a far deeper understanding of the task: it identifies the official “terminal-bench” reference, inspects and runs the real grader, writes a zero-dependency Node.js ELF parser that guarantees 100% coverage, and exhaustively tests against PIE, non-PIE, and static binaries. Transcript 2 offers only a cursory PT_LOAD extractor without section analysis or rigorous validation.

Transcript 2 demonstrates a much deeper end-to-end solution: it identifies the task origin in the terminal-bench repo, fetches and inspects the official reference solution and test harness, crafts a superset extractor to guarantee zero mismatches and full coverage, patches and tests iteratively against multiple binary variants, and provides a comprehensive summary. Transcript 1, while correct, only writes and lightly tests an ELF parser without integrating the actual grader’s reference or validating against it.

Transcript 1 shows a systematic, automated approach with scripting, parallel evaluation, clear verification of only allowed synonym swaps, and rigorous zero-warning proof. Transcript 2 is ad-hoc, manual, error-prone and never truly eliminates all warnings. Transcript 1 is from the more capable model.

Transcript 2 is produced by the more capable model. It adopts a clear plan, automates the synonym‐search via a parallelized greedy search script in Perl, converges in three iterations, and rigorously verifies the final result with diffs and checks. Transcript 1 is a much more ad‐hoc, error‐prone manual trial‐and‐error process.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a deep, methodical forensic recovery, including overlay filesystem analysis, binary carving of fragmented ZIP structures, CRC validation, and full ZIP reconstruction. Transcript 2 resorts to trial-and-error grepping and partial extraction without rigor or verification.

Transcript 2 demonstrates a structured, systematic forensic methodology—identifying ZIP signatures, extracting and reconstructing fragmented ZIP headers, verifying CRC32 integrity, and confirming the recovered password’s format—whereas Transcript 1 resorts to brute‐force grepping and ad hoc attempts. The thorough reconstruction and verification in Transcript 2 reflect the higher capability.

Transcript 1 is methodical and concise, performing targeted scans for AWS, GitHub, and Hugging Face tokens, applying precise replacements, verifying each change, and summarizing the results clearly. Transcript 2 is verbose, unfocused, and repeats scanning steps without a clear completion.

Transcript 2 delivers a clear, focused workflow: it identifies exactly the affected files, applies precise `sed` commands to replace secrets with the proper placeholders, and then immediately verifies via rescans and syntax checks. Transcript 1, by contrast, is overly verbose and expansively scans and rewrites many files with a complex ad hoc script, making it less efficient and targeted.

Transcript 1 shows a systematic, data-driven development process—profiling classic warriors, building a test harness, iteratively tuning decoy counts and SPL parameters, verifying both fixed-series and random-position performance, and converging on a robust CoreWars warrior that meets all thresholds. Transcript 2 is much more ad-hoc, with broken variants, no rigorous tuning or verification, and only a superficial final submission. Transcript 1 is clearly from the more capable model.

Transcript 2 shows systematic exploration of the problem, building matchup matrices, writing and tuning many warrior variants, and using rigorous statistical testing (fixed and random positions) to converge on a robust solution. It presents clear reasoning, structured experiments, and final verification steps. Transcript 1 is superficial trial-and-error with many dead ends and unfocused code iterations.
